claims.claim: H.R. 9340 defines a large-load customer by facilities that require electric energy primarily to operate information technology infrastructure for data storage and computational applications.
claims.verbatim: require electric energy primarily to operate information technology infrastructure and related systems pertaining to data storage and computational applications and services
claims.notes: Engrossed in House text, re-fetched live and matched to saved hr9340_eh.txt. The source wraps across lines, and line breaks are collapsed here. The definition never uses the words data center.

claims.claim: Under H.R. 9340 the large-load threshold is an aggregate peak demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus.
claims.verbatim: have, in the aggregate, a peak electric demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus
claims.notes: This is peak demand, which is power, not annual energy. The wording is unchanged from the reported version checked in run 2026-09-13 (C05).

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 applies the large-load definition only to non-residential consumers who request or enter a contract on or after enactment.
claims.value: on or after the date of the enactment
claims.verbatim: means a non-residential electric consumer that, on or after the date of the enactment of this paragraph, requests to enter into, or enters into, a contract or other agreement
claims.notes: Forward looking only. Line breaks are collapsed, including the hyphenated line break in "non-residential".

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 says rates to a large-load customer shall be designed to recover the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission or distribution upgrade needed to serve it.
claims.verbatim: shall be designed to recover from the large-load customer the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve the load of such large-load customer
claims.notes: needs_softening true. This is the text of a PURPA standard that states must CONSIDER (C47, C48). It is not a direct federal mandate on rates. Write "would set a standard", never "requires data centers to pay".

claims.claim: The H.R. 9340 cost recovery standard covers the case of a large-load customer terminating its contract or ceasing to buy power.
claims.verbatim: including in the event of such large-load customer terminating a contract or other agreement with the electric utility pertaining to the sale of electric energy, or otherwise ceasing the purchase of electric energy from the electric utility
claims.notes: This is the stranded-asset clause.

claims.claim: Under the H.R. 9340 standard a utility must require financial assurances or contributions from a large-load customer before making an upgrade to serve it.
claims.verbatim: Before making any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade that is necessary to serve the load of a large-load customer, an electric utility shall require the large-load customer provide to the electric utility financial assurances or contributions to cover the cost of such upgrade.
claims.notes: The verbatim runs 44 words, slightly over the 40-word guide. Trim it to "an electric utility shall require the large-load customer provide to the electric utility financial assurances or contributions to cover the cost of such upgrade" if needed. Same softening as C44, since this is part of the standard states consider.

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 gives each State regulatory authority 1 year after enactment to commence consideration of the standard or set a hearing date.
claims.verbatim: Not later than 1 year after the date of enactment of this paragraph, each State regulatory authority
claims.notes: Conditional on enactment, and the bill is not law. Write "would". No calendar date can be attached.

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 gives each State regulatory authority 2 years after enactment to complete consideration and make a determination on the standard.
claims.verbatim: Not later than 2 years after the date of enactment of this paragraph, each State regulatory authority
claims.notes: The obligation is to complete the consideration and make the determination. Nothing compels a state to adopt the standard, and this is the substance behind the Democratic "optional" criticism.

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 exempts a state from the consideration clocks if, before enactment, the state has implemented the standard or a comparable standard.
claims.verbatim: the State has implemented for the electric utility the standard (or a comparable standard)
claims.notes: This is prong 1 of the "Other Prior State Actions" subsection, which says subsections (b) and (c) shall not apply "if, before the date of enactment of this subsection".

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 also exempts a state whose regulatory authority has conducted a proceeding to consider implementing the standard before enactment.
claims.verbatim: has conducted a proceeding to consider implementation of the standard (or a comparable standard) for the electric utility
claims.notes: Prong 2. Whether the Regulatory Commission of Alaska has run such a proceeding is still unverified in either direction (killed in run 2026-09-13).

claims.claim: H.R. 9340 also exempts a state where the state legislature has voted on implementing the standard or a comparable one before enactment.
claims.verbatim: the State legislature has voted on the implementation of the standard (or a comparable standard) for the electric utility
claims.notes: needs_softening true when applied to Alaska. Whether one chamber's vote (C59, C60) counts as "the State legislature has voted", and whether SB 250 is a "comparable standard", is unresolved. Pose it as a question.

claims.claim: In floor remarks on September 29th, Schumer said that all Republicans offer on AI and data centers is a toothless messaging bill.

Say Schumer attacked "the Republican data center bill". Don't say he was speaking about H.R. 9340 itself. Same page: "A guardrail that is optional isn't a guardrail at all."

claims.claim: Alaska law empowers the Regulatory Commission of Alaska to make or require just, fair and reasonable rates for a public utility.
claims.verbatim: make or require just, fair, and reasonable rates, classifications, regulations, practices, services, and facilities for a public utility
claims.notes: Fetched through r.jina.ai. Together with C65, this supports calling the RCA the state regulatory authority that would do the H.R. 9340 consideration for regulated Alaska utilities. That last step is an inference, so write "would likely fall to".

claims.claim: Alaska law sets the Legislature to convene at the capital each year on the third Tuesday in January at 1 p.m.
claims.verbatim: The legislature shall convene at the capital each year on the third Tuesday in January at 1:00 p.m.
claims.notes: Fetched through r.jina.ai, twice. The second fetch printed the full body and reported no exception or proviso. Odd years hold the First Regular Session.

claims.claim: The third Tuesday in January 2027 falls on January 19th, 2027, the statutory convening date of the next Alaska Legislature.
claims.verbatim: on the third Tuesday in January at 1:00 p.m.
claims.notes: Derived. January 1st, 2027 is a Friday, so the Tuesdays fall on January 5th, 12th and 19th, and the third is the 19th. No official 2027 calendar was reached. Write "set by statute to convene January 19th, 2027", because the legislature can change it.

claims.claim: Alaska's general election falls on Tuesday, November 3rd.
claims.verbatim: Election Day Tuesday, November 3
claims.notes: Fetched live. Corroborated by States Newsroom (Jacob Fischler) in the same Beacon feed, October 1st: "before the Nov. 3 elections that will determine control of Congress". November 3rd, 2026 is a Tuesday.

stories_surviving: H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, blocked in the U.S. Senate on September 30th (update of Carousel No.58)

killed.claim: Schumer said "We need real action on data centres, and what do Republicans decide all of a sudden to push forward? A bill that is totally optional."
killed.why: This wording is on Al Jazeera only. Schumer's own published floor remarks of September 29th render the line differently ("Here we need some real actions on data centers, and what does the Republican Senator from Ohio come up with: something that is optional."). A named person's quote with two conflicting versions can't be used verbatim. If needed, use C57's primary text.

killed.claim: H.R. 9340 failed to require data centers to cover the costs of grid upgrades.
killed.why: This is Al Jazeera's paraphrase of Schumer, a one-sided framing. The bill text sets a standard that rates be designed to recover the full, incremental cost (C44), but it obliges states only to consider and determine (C48). It may be used only as an attributed criticism, never as a fact.

killed.claim: Schumer's September 29th floor remarks were about H.R. 9340.
killed.why: The remarks never name H.R. 9340 or the Ratepayer Protection Act. They point to a bill by "the Republican Senator from Ohio", which matches S. 5028 (Husted). Linking them to the House bill is an inference.

killed.claim: The Senate vote on H.R. 9340 took place at 12:51 p.m.
killed.why: Killed in this unqualified form. The Senate XML's 12:51 PM conflicts with the BILLSTATUS recorded timestamp of 1:45 p.m. Eastern. Only the softened C07 survives.

killed.claim: Rep. Nick Begich's first name, and the first names Summer Lee, Delia Ramirez and Rashida Tlaib, as printed on the House roll.
killed.why: The Clerk's roll prints surnames only. First names come from bioguide IDs I did not fetch. Begich is safe as Alaska's sole representative. For the three nays, use surname and state unless the showrunner confirms first names.
